title: Family music and the first clarinet
summary: Sisters played piano, an uncle was a country fiddler; Kelly learned from records and a neighbor boy, and bought an Albert System clarinet for $36.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: And were they musicals at Browning?

Well, my two sisters both played piano, but they just studied it and played, you know, very well. All girls at that time were supposed to take piano, so they did. I had one great uncle who was a country fiddler, and then as far as my Irish ancestors were playing, they were musical people too. Nobody in the family we knew. Nobody in the family we knew particularly musical.
They did play well. Do you remember the names of any of them?

Well, the country fiddler was my Uncle Gus Clayton. And he was a Mississippi and played four dances out in the country, you know, just like those square dances and things like that. My father was often worried. He'd say, there you go. You're going to be like Uncle Gus, playing that music. They were not particularly interested in having me play, but my sisters were all far and my mother died when I was very young. And I became interested in playing. We had a school, East End School band in Marshall. And I had been listening to records, Art Hickman, original Dixeland Jazz Band, Louisiana, and other, Old Wilber C. Sweatman, different recordings. We didn't have a patrol, but the neighbors across the street had one, had a wonderful selection record. So I just became interested in it that way. And it started very young. And I played, actually, ordered a clarinet from Charlie Parker in Houston, the band director that came out in the barns park, even in those days. In fact, the little towns didn't have the music stuff to an extent. They had to be ordered from Houston or Dallas. And so, the day I got my clarinet, one of the neighbor boys, Harold Atkins, already played the clarinet. He came by the house and showed me the fingering and I could play the clarinet. And I started like that.
Did you have, could you play by ear or were you?

Yeah. He showed me the fingering and I could play immediately because I had, of course I had played on the king flutes and which is similar to our modern fluter fans. So, I just was kind of extremely interested from the beginning.
Well, since you know so much about instruments, I assume, you're in the business. What kind of clarinet was it? Do you have any idea?

Well, the first clarinet, and I think this is an interesting story. I've told him a lot of times, but it's true. The band director came around to the kids and said, I can get you an Albert System clarinet for $36. I can get you an Albert System clarinet, that's the new kind, for $80. And I had the $36 and I didn't have the $80, so I didn't know the difference. I took the Albert and I've always played the same thing. But the name of the clarinet, the first one I ever had was a Henry Gunkel. G-U-N-K-E-L, which came from Charlie Park in Houston. It was just one of any number of names which were used on clarinet. The distributors only put a name on most of them. For their cheap instruments, they'll use a local name, just like Whirlines, very often have stenciled instruments under their own name, the band for the New York Clans.
So it was a fairly simple thing, fairly close to the can read.
